For example, similar to the H-2B and CW-1 temporary labor certification programs, this proposal would require submission of the employer’s recruitment report for CO review before the CO issues a final determination.67 However, the timing of recruitment report submission before final determination would be different, based on when required recruitment activities are completed—pre-filing for the PERM labor certification program and during application review for the H-2B and CW-1 programs. Because recruitment—and a final recruitment report—must be completed pre-filing, requiring submission of the employer’s recruitment report at the time of filing the Application for Permanent Employment Certification is an appropriate programmatic difference, which furthers the Department’s processing efficiency goals. As proposed for the PERM labor certification program, the CO would be able to review employers’ NOFs and recruitment reports—and related 67 See 20 CFR 655.48 and 655.446.
supporting documentation—before reaching final determinations without additional, unnecessary correspondence.

Timeliness for filing The Department is proposing a single filing timeframe requirement for submission of Applications for Permanent Employment Certification to OFLC in proposed section 656.10(b). An employer would be required to submit the complete Application for Permanent Employment Certification, with all documentation and information required at the time of filing, within 30 calendar days after the employer completes all pre-filing recruitment requirements. Together with proposed section 656.17(d), this would mean an employer must complete all recruitment activities between 30 to 60 calendar days before the employer expects to file the Application for Permanent Employment Certification and then file the application between 1 and 29 calendar days after the last recruitment activity ends. This 30-day timing requirement would apply to both employers who engage in the pre-filing recruitment procedures set forth in proposed section 656.17 and employers who engage in the optional pre-filing recruitment procedures for college and university teachers or professional athletes and professional sports team coaches set forth in proposed section 656.18. Currently, employers filing under section 656.17 must submit the application within 180 calendar days of beginning pre-filing recruitment activities and NOF posting, while employers filing under section 656.18 must do so within 18 months of the alien’s selection, which is often many months before the actual filing of the application.68 The Department proposes this filing timeframe change to simplify part 656 and better provide the CO with more current information about the availability of U.S. workers for job opportunities that are the subject of an Application for Permanent Employment Certification. Under the current rule, an employer’s recruitment and 68 See 20 CFR 656.10(d)(3)(iv); 656.17(e)(1)(i) and (ii); 656.17(e)(2); and 656.18(c). recruitment results can become stale before the employer submits its Application for Permanent Employment Certification. The Department considers the current timeframes—180 calendar days and 18 months in current sections 656.17 and 656.18, respectively—longer than necessary to enable employers to prepare their recruitment reports after completing pre-filing recruitment requirements. The Department considers the proposed 30-day timeframe after completion of pre-filing recruitment to be a reasonable period for preparation of recruitment reports for submission with the Application for Permanent Employment Certification and those recruitment reports would provide better information about the current availability of U.S. workers to the CO. In addition, as proposed, employers would file the Application for Permanent Employment Certification in closer proximity to the labor market test, which would ensure that U.S. workers who may have availability for the job opportunity are made aware of the job in closer proximity to the filing of the Application for Permanent Employment Certification, rather than many months ahead of time, and the recruitment report provided to the CO reflects current labor market results.

The Department invites comments on the proposed filing timeframe requirement that is consistent with the Department’s goal of simplifying part 656 and ensuring recruitment activities and the report of recruitment results are not stale when submitted to the NPC. In particular, the Department invites comments about whether the 30-day timeliness requirement should be applied to Applications for Permanent Employment Certification filed using the proposed competitive recruitment and selection process of proposed section 656.18 based on the last advertisement date or the date of the organizational or administrative body’s final report making the recommendation or selection of the alien. See proposed section 656.18(a)(2).

Location and method of filing In paragraph (c), the Department proposes to require electronic filing for Applications for Permanent Employment Certification submitted to OFLC, except in limited circumstances. This proposal does not constitute a change for those employers who file Applications for Permanent Employment Certification using the Department’s FLAG system, available at https://flag.dol.gov/. FLAG continues to be the OFLC Administrator’s designated electronic filing method for Applications for Permanent Employment Certification. Consistent with the Department’s approach when mandating electronic filing in temporary labor certification programs, the Department proposes similar procedures in the PERM labor certification program under paragraphs (c)(2) and (3), through which an employer may request authorization to file by mail by demonstrating to the OFLC Administrator that they are unable or limited in their ability to use or access electronic filing. An employer may contact the NPC in writing to the address designated in a notice published in the Federal Register, or for individuals with hearing or speech impairments, 1-877-889-5627 (this is the TTY toll-free Federal Information Relay Service number) for assistance in using, accessing, or filing any form or documentation required under this part, including the Application for Permanent Employment Certification. This proposal—and the parallel proposal in section 656.40(a)(2) to require electronic filing for Applications for Prevailing Wage Determination—would bring consistency across the foreign labor certification and labor condition application programs administered by the Department. If adopted, employers would submit all applications electronically to OFLC through the FLAG system, unless a limited exception applied.

Based on extensive experience administering permanent and temporary labor certification programs, the Department has determined that mandating electronic filing reduces costs (e.g., mailing fees) and burdens for most employers and for the Department, reduces the frequency of delays related to filing applications, improves the quality of information collected, promotes administrative efficiency and accountability, and increases consistency across labor certification programs. For employers and their authorized representatives, the Department’s proposal to require electronic filing would improve customer experience by permitting more prompt processing of applications and reducing paperwork burdens and mailing costs. Electronic filing provides system prompts, which include warnings that an application is incomplete or obviously inaccurate and provides employers with an immediate opportunity to correct the errors or upload the missing documentation. Mandatory electronic filing furthers efficiency in communications between the Department and the employer and its representatives. The Department anticipates that requiring e-filing will not require a change of practice for the vast majority of employers. Based on fiscal year (FY) 2021-FY 2025 data, approximately 99.61 percent of PERM labor certification applications were filed electronically.69 Almost all of the remaining 0.39 percent of PERM labor certification applications filed by mail also disclosed valid email addresses on the application form, thereby suggesting that employers and, if applicable, their authorized attorneys and agents have access to the internet and are likely capable of filing electronically. Additional documentation required for certain applications After eliminating the content of current paragraph (e), as discussed below, the Department proposes to repurpose paragraph (e) to address additional documentation requirements for certain job opportunities. The Department proposes to relocate the content of current sections 656.19(b) (documentation for live-in household domestic service workers) and 656.17(l) (documentation related to alien influence over the job opportunity) to proposed sections 656.10(e)(1) and (e)(2), respectively, and add new regulatory content in proposed section 656.10(e)(3) to codify, with minor changes, the 69 DOL OFLC Performance data for fiscal years 2021 through 2025 available at https://www.dol.gov/agencies/eta/foreign-labor/performance (last accessed May 6, 2026). current practice for employers seeking to permanently employ professional athletes or professional sports team coaches, who meet the definition set forth in section 656.3. After relocating the content of current section 656.19(b) to proposed section 656.10(e)(1), the Department proposes non-substantive changes for readability and changes to simplify documentation, while better ensuring the employment contract fully discloses all appropriate information about live-in household domestic service jobs offered. Under the current rule, the employer must prepare and retain both a statement describing the household living accommodations, which contains the information listed in current section 656.19(b)(1), and an employment contract, which contains information listed in current section 656.19(b)(2). The proposed rule would eliminate the separate statement describing household living accommodations and relocate its required content to the employment contract, resulting in one document that contains all required information about the job offered. This proposal simplifies documentation requirements, while better ensuring that the alien is apprised of the household living accommodations information. In addition, the proposed rule would reduce the number of copies of the employment contract the employer must retain. Currently, an employer seeking to permanently employ an alien in a live-in household domestic service job opportunity must retain two copies of the employment contract, but the proposed rule would only require retention of one.70 The Department’s proposed section 656.10(e)(1)(i) eliminates two key pieces of information from the content required of employment contracts for live-in household domestic service job opportunity (i.e., the wage offer and description of duties required under current section 656.19(b)(2)(i) and (v), respectively). However, the two pieces of information are still required. The proposed language that introduces the enumerated list in proposed section 656.10(e)(1)(i) states that the employment contract must “contain[], 70 Compare current section 656.19(b)(2) (“Two copies”), with proposed section 656.10(e)(1)(i) (“A copy”). at a minimum, the same material terms of employment specified on the Application for Permanent Employment Certification and the following information and employment guarantees.” By requiring the employment contract to contain the same material terms of employment as the Application for Permanent Employment Certification, the Department ensures not only that the employment contract will continue to contain the wage offer and description of duties, but also any other material terms of employment the employer specified on the Application for Permanent Employment Certification, which could not be adequately captured in a static list. Moreover, through this approach, the Department would better ensure that the employment contract contains all essential information and is consistent with the Application for Permanent Employment Certification used to test the U.S. labor market.

Proposed section 656.10(e)(2) retains content of the additional documentation requirements found in current section 656.17(l) (Alien influence and control over job opportunity) with one change to simplify the rule by eliminating redundant language and, otherwise, only minor changes to conform with terminology used throughout this proposed rule. Proposed section 656.10(e)(2) eliminates the phrase “must be able to demonstrate the existence of a bona fide job opportunity, i.e., the job is available to all U.S. workers,” which appears in current section 656.17(l). This is not a requirement limited to job opportunities involving closely held corporations or partnerships in which the alien has an ownership interest; or familial relationships between the stockholders, corporate officers, incorporators, or partners, and the alien; or the alien as one of a small number of employees. It is a requirement applicable to all Applications for Permanent Employment Certification under both the current and proposed rules. The current rule addresses the requirement in section 656.10(c)(8) as well as section 656.17(l), while the proposed rule addresses this requirement in proposed section 656.13(a).

Under proposed section 656.10(e)(3), employers filing Applications for Permanent Employment Certification for professional athletes or professional sports team coaches would be required to prepare and maintain the following documentation, consistent with longstanding practice: (1) a copy of the executed written contract, signed and dated by the employer and alien, covering the entire year or period that indicates the specific payment(s) made to the alien; (2) an employment letter stating that the alien will work a minimum of ten (10) hours per week during the off-season period; and (3) for an alien being sponsored for permanent employment as a professional athlete, a copy of a letter or response, whether electronic or print, from the Players’ Association (e.g., NBA, NHL, NFL, MLB) or applicable trade union(s) stating that it was provided notice from the employer, as required by section 656.14(a)(1), and has no objection to the filing of the Application for Permanent Employment Certification. The Department recognizes that Players’ Association and trade union(s) may vary in their responsiveness to an employer’s notice and request for confirmation of “no objection” to the filing of an Application for Permanent Employment Certification. The Department invites comments about whether and how an employer could document compliance with this notice and request requirement, in the absence of a response from the Players’ Association or applicable trade union(s).

The Department does not propose to change the timing of submission for this additional documentation. Employers filing applications subject to the additional documentation requirements under proposed section 656.10(e) would continue to prepare and maintain the additional documentation required for the job opportunity in their record retention file and only submit it upon request. However, by locating the additional documentation requirements in proposed section 656.10, the Department clarifies that— both currently and under the proposed rule—preparation and retention of the additional documentation is a filing requirement, meaning it must be prepared and already saved in the employer’s record retention file at the time of Application for Permanent Employment Certification submission. No new burden would be incurred by employers as a result of this change.

Filing date The Department proposes to relocate the filing date provision currently in section 656.17(c) to the centralized filing requirements in proposed section 656.10(f), with modifications to conform with other proposed regulatory changes herein. The proposed paragraph continues to deem the date OFLC accepts for processing a complete Application for Permanent Employment Certification to be the “filing date.” For an electronically filed application, the “filing date” is the date the application is submitted and accepted in the electronic system based on the time of acceptance in the Eastern time zone of the United States. For an application submitted by mail under the procedures proposed at section 656.10(c)(2) and (3), the “filing date” would be the postmark date affixed to the employer’s Application for Permanent Employment Certification submission, provided that the NPC determines the application is complete. This would be a change for applications submitted by mail. Currently, the filing date is the date the NPC accepts the application for processing and affixes a date stamp on the submission. However, the current approach is less straightforward than establishing the filing date using the postmark and delay between delivery and affixing a date stamp has resulted in denials for noncompliance with timing requirements (e.g., recruitment dates within the 180 days prior to the filing date) that BALCA has overturned.71 In the interest of simplicity, efficiency, and certainty, the Department proposes to use the postmark date as the filing date for complete applications submitted by mail.

Completeness 71 E.g., Dorbin Metal Strip Manufacturing Co., Inc., 2022-PER-00043 (Dec. 26, 2023) (remanding application for further processing when a delay in date stamping caused the application to be untimely). Current section 656.17(a)(1) provides that incomplete applications will be denied. In the proposed section 656.10(g), the Department proposes, instead, to return incomplete applications to employers unprocessed.

Under the proposed rule, a complete application consists of a Form ETA-9089, Application for Permanent Employment Certification, with all required fields completed with valid information, a valid PWD, and the employer’s recruitment report for the job opportunity offered on the Application for Permanent Employment Certification, as outlined in proposed section 656.10(a). Despite form instructions and FLAG system prompts designed to ensure employers submit complete Applications for Permanent Employment Certification, the Department receives applications missing required information. The Department has received applications where the employer overrode system prompts or entered nonsensical or placeholder information (e.g., the employer’s point of contact as a movie or cartoon character or “TBD” (to be determined) or “Test Subject” as the alien’s name) in order to circumvent system prompts meant to ensure only complete, valid applications are submitted. The Department anticipates that it will continue to receive such applications, which slow processing of legitimate, complete applications filed by employers with a genuine need for workers. With this rule’s proposed addition of the employer’s recruitment report and other recruitment related documentation as an application filing requirement, the Department also anticipates that an unscrupulous employer may try to circumvent these requirements by uploading into FLAG something other than their recruitment documentation to likewise evade system checks. Without, for example, a valid recruitment report or documentation demonstrating compliance with the advertising requirements or a signed Form ETA-9089, Appendix E, the application will be deemed incomplete.

Under the proposed rule, incomplete Applications for Permanent Employment Certification submitted to the NPC will not be processed. Rather, when an incomplete Application for Permanent Employment Certification is discovered—which would occur when the application is assigned to an analyst for review, as provided in proposed section 656.19(a)—the NPC would return the application unprocessed. As the CO will not reach any substantive determinations before returning an incomplete application unprocessed, proposed section 656.10(g) clarifies that an employer cannot request reconsideration or review pursuant to section 656.26 after an application is returned by the NPC unprocessed due to incompleteness. In addition, the “filing date” of the incomplete application would not be retained and cannot be claimed for purposes of establishing a priority date. Rather, the employer may file a new Application for Permanent Employment Certification that is complete and satisfies all requirements of part 656 and the filing date would be the date the NPC accepts the new complete application for processing, in accordance with proposed section 656.10(f).

The Department recognizes that the proposed consequences for submission of an incomplete application are more strict than under the current rule. However, in light of the Administration’s broad efforts to combat visa fraud and abuse and ensure the broadest pool of qualified U.S. workers have fair access to these job opportunities before a permanent labor certification is granted, the Department considers the consequences appropriate to safeguard limited resources and facilitate the processing of complete, genuinely filed applications.

Likewise, recognizing the consequence of returning an application unprocessed, the Department only intends to exercise this authority in situations where it is clear that the application is incomplete. For example, when a document other than the recruitment report is submitted, when the included PWD is invalid, when the employer is listed as a fictional entity, or when required fields include placeholders like “TBD.” This provision is not intended to allow the Department to make substantive denials without permitting reconsideration or review by BALCA. The provision is intended to permit OFLC to avoid spending time reviewing and drafting denials for applications which fail to meet the basic standards of a legitimate, complete application.

Record retention requirements The Department proposes to retain the employer’s record retention requirements, but it is seeking to relocate this provision from current section 656.10(f) to proposed section 656.10(h), with a change to the timeframe that would be required for employers to retain all documentation. Currently, employers are required to retain a copy of the Application for Permanent Employment Certification and all supporting documentation to demonstrate compliance with program requirements for a 5-year period, with the 5- year period beginning on the date the Application for Permanent Employment Certification was filed. The Department proposes to retain the 5-year period of retention, but to count the 5-year period of retention from the date on which the Immigrant Petition is approved, denied, or withdrawn. If the employer does not proceed to file an Immigrant Petition, it would be required to retain all records associated with the Application for Permanent Employment Certification for a period of 5 years from the expiration of the labor certification or the date of denial or withdrawal.

The current record retention timeframe overlaps with application processing timeframes and, in doing so, it fails to provide a full 5-year record retention period. By starting the record retention clock with the final determination for denied or withdrawn applications or the expiration of a certified application, or from the date on which the Immigrant Petition, if any, is approved, denied, or withdrawn, essential records will be available for the full period intended, which allows the Department, and other partner agencies, to request and obtain these records, if necessary, in order to conduct further review, investigations or any integrity actions.

Applicability of section 656.10 The Department reiterates for clarity that the filing procedures proposed in section 656.10 would apply to all employers required to obtain a PERM labor certification from OFLC for purposes of submitting an I-140 petition to USCIS. This would include job opportunities currently covered under Schedule A and certain sheepherders, consistent with the Department’s proposals to eliminate current alternative regulatory procedures at sections 656.15 (Schedule A) and 656.16 (Sheepherders).

With this proposed change, employers seeking to permanently hire aliens to perform job opportunities currently defined as Schedule A or as qualifying sheepherders under part 656 would continue to obtain a PWD from OFLC but, going forward, also would be required to engage in pre-filing recruitment and submit their application to OFLC, rather than to USCIS, along with their recruitment report.

Similarly, the filing requirements in proposed section 656.10 would apply to employers seeking to permanently employ aliens as professional athletes or professional sports team coaches in job opportunities subject to the EB-2 or EB-3 visa classifications requirements, including those currently covered by Schedule A, which would require a PERM labor certification under this proposed rule.72 Eliminated provision The Department proposes to eliminate section 656.10(e) of the current rule in its entirety. The proposed elimination of current section 656.10(e) is consistent with the Department’s goal of simplifying its PERM program regulations.

Current section 656.10(e)(1) states that the public may submit evidence to the CO that may have bearing on an Application for Permanent Employment Certification. This provision duplicates the function of the NOF, which similarly invites any person to 72 The proposed rule, including section 656.10, does not apply to all professional athletes. Some professional athletes may be eligible for the EB-1 visa classification based on extraordinary ability in athletics or a national interest waiver of the EB-2 permanent labor certification requirement. See 8 CFR 204.5(h)(1) Compliance with part 656 is not required for those job opportunities. provide information or other documentation bearing on an Application for Permanent Employment Certification to OFLC for consideration in reaching the determinations required for PERM labor certification. See proposed section 656.14(d). The type of information or other documentation to be submitted to OFLC using the contact information provided in the NOF is the same as that described in current 656.10(e)(1)— information on available workers, information on wages and working conditions, and information on the employer's failure to meet the terms and conditions for the employment of aliens and similarly employed workers. In addition, as discussed below in connection with the Department’s proposed expansion of NOF visibility, the proposed elimination of current section 656.10(e)(1) would simplify the regulation without impact to program integrity.

The Department also proposes to eliminate current section 656.10(e)(2), which discusses the submission of evidence to DHS. Although the Department is aware that DHS accepts and considers such information, the elimination of current section 656.10(e)(2) is consistent with the Department’s intent to simplify part 656 by eliminating regulatory content that discusses another agency’s processes.
2. Proposed 20 CFR 656.11, Substitutions and modifications to applications.

In this rulemaking, the Department proposes to retain current section 656.11’s prohibitions on substituting aliens and modifying Applications for Permanent Employment Certification, with revisions to update terminology, eliminate outdated language, and improve clarity. For example, proposed revisions replace “application” with “Application for Permanent Employment Certification,” among other minor revisions.

The Department also proposes removing references to July 16, 2007, which are no longer necessary. Prior to the establishment of current section 656.11, the Department allowed employers to substitute an alien named on a permanent labor certification with another prospective alien. Labor certification substitution occurred either while the PERM labor certification application was pending with the Department or, by the Department’s delegation to DHS, when a Form I-140 petition was submitted or was pending with DHS based on an approved PERM labor certification. This practice was permitted due to the length of time it took to obtain a PERM labor certification and Form I-140 petition approval.

On May 17, 2007, the Department issued the Final Rule, Labor Certification for the Permanent Employment of Aliens in the United States; Reducing the Incentives and Opportunities for Fraud and Abuse and Enhancing Program Integrity (“2007 Fraud Rule”), through which the Department eliminated the practice of allowing the substitution of aliens on PERM labor certifications through rulemaking.73 In the 2007 Fraud Rule, the Department established that substitution or change to the identity of an alien was prohibited on any application filed with the Department for PERM labor certification and on any resulting certification.74 See current 20 CFR 656.11(a). The 2007 rule also revised current section 656.30(c)(2) to state that a PERM labor certification is only valid for the alien named on the original PERM labor certification application.75 Further, the 2007 Fraud Rule clarified that requests for modifications to an application, where the application was filed after the final rule’s effective date, would not be accepted. See current 20 CFR 656.11(b). The Department explained that it had implemented technological changes in the PERM program to alert applicants to technical grounds for deniability, thus eliminating the need for many modifications.76 73 See current 20 CFR 656.11.

The Department has no intention of changing section 656.11(b) to permit substantive changes to an Application for Permanent Employment Certification, while in process or after certification, if certified. A substantive change is one that would correct an error that would lead to denial, if not corrected. The employer has the burden of proof to establish eligibility for a PERM labor certification and the responsibility to submit a complete and accurate Application for Permanent Employment Certification.

The Department has considered how it might appropriately permit minor modifications to an Application for Permanent Employment Certification while it is pending with the NPC. By minor modifications, the Department refers to errors that have no bearing on the CO’s assessment of the employer’s compliance with program requirements. An error is not minor—and its correction would not be a minor modification—if its correction would prevent denial. In addition, the Department has no interest in permitting correction of errors that clearly could have been prevented with closer attention, such as ridiculous errors (e.g., place holders or cartoon characters) or multiple errors—even if arguably clerical—in the same application. Rather, the Department would consider allowing correction of isolated instances of purely clerical errors for which correction could be appropriate to avoid wasted resources of withdrawing and refiling for both the employer and the NPC.

The Department invites comments about whether part 656 should be revised to permit any minor modifications and, if so, the conditions under which minor modifications could be permitted without impact to program integrity or program efficiency. Helpful comments will discuss time period limitations for requesting a minor modification (e.g., within the 30 calendar days after filing or prior to the issuance of a final determination by the CO); the scope of minor modifications with examples (e.g., correcting a birthdate, visa classification or phone number for the alien or replacing an agent or attorney information with a new representative’s information) and identifying form fields that do not contain substantive information, as substantive information could not be modified.
3. Proposed 20 CFR 656.12, Improper commerce and payment.

Through the 2007 Fraud Rule, the Department imposed clear limitations on the acquisition and use of a pending or approved permanent labor certification application to reduce the incentives and opportunities for fraud and abuse in the permanent labor certification program and to propose measures to enhance the integrity of the permanent labor certification program.77 The 2007 Fraud Rule revised section 656.12(a) to create a complete ban on the sale, barter, and purchase of labor certification applications and certifications. The revisions applied to applications filed on or after the effective date of the 2007 Fraud Rule regardless of whether the labor certification application involved was filed under the regulations of 20 CFR part 656 in effect before March 28, 2005, or, on or after, March 28, 2005.78 Under this proposed rule, the Department proposes to eliminate the transition procedures in the introductory part of section 656.12 related to the 2004 PERM Final Rule79 and the 2007 Fraud Rule because the transition procedures in this section are obsolete.

The current section 656.12 states that it applies to applications “under this part” and “certifications resulting from those applications,” while stating in sections 656.12(a) and (c) that those provisions only apply to “approved permanent labor certifications.” The Department’s proposed introductory language serves to clarify that the provisions of section 656.12 apply to any Application for Permanent Employment Certification and any PERM labor certification. The proposed terminology changes serve to better frame the scope of various possible outcomes for Applications for Permanent Employment 77 See 72 FR 27903 (May 17, 2007).
78 See 72 FR 27903, 27907 (May 17, 2007). This rule became effective on July 16, 2007. 79 See 69 FR 77326 (Dec. 27, 2004).

Certification (e.g., certification, withdrawal, invalidation, revocation) and continue to place employers on notice that their Applications for Permanent Employment Certification and PERM labor certifications under part 656 are subject to the provisions of section 656.12.
4. Proposed New 20 CFR 656.13, Assurances and obligations of employers.

The Department is proposing the creation of a new section at 656.13 to enumerate by topic the assurances and obligations under the PERM program to which an employer must attest compliance. Organizing all existing and newly proposed required attestations into one section will improve clarity and navigation within part 656 and part 656 with similar regulatory provisions the Department has in the H-1B, H-2A and H-2B programs.80 By clearly stating the employer’s legal obligations in one provision of the regulations, the Department has determined this approach will make it easier for employers to find, understand, and comply with the program requirements. Further, the proposed changes in section 656.13 would enhance protections for U.S. workers, including protection of U.S. worker wages, and promote consideration of U.S. workers for job opportunities, notably by expanding contact and consideration requirements in layoff situations and preventing employers from laying off U.S. workers to create the perception of available vacancies and filing an Application for Permanent Employment Certification with the intention of replacing laid off U.S. workers with aliens. See proposed 656.13(e) and (f).

For proposed section 656.13, employers will be required to read and agree to comply with essential program requirements and worker protections for both U.S. and aliens when submitting an application under part 656, which will improve program integrity. Under penalty of perjury, employers will attest that they have read and 80 See 20 CFR 655.20 and 20 CFR 655.135.

reviewed every page of the Application for Permanent Employment Certification, including all applicable appendices and supporting documentation, and to the best of their knowledge the information contained therein is true and accurate. In addition, employers will assure they understand that knowingly and/or willfully furnishing materially false information in the preparation of this form and any supplement thereto or to aid, abet, or counsel another to do so is a federal offense punishable by fines, imprisonment, or both under 18 U.S.C. §§ 2, 1001, 1546, 1621. The clearer requirements will also enhance the Department’s program integrity efforts, as clearer requirements provide a more straightforward path for enforcement of program requirements.

Specifically, the Department is proposing to take existing required attestations, currently codified at section 656.10(c), and replace and relocate them to this new proposed section 656.13, while further replacing the language of the existing attestations to strengthen program integrity. The Department proposes to replace and relocate regulatory content explaining the nature and effect of attestations from current section 656.10(c) to the introductory language of proposed section 656.13. In addition, the Department is proposing to relocate other existing obligations from current sections 656.10, 656.12, 656.17, and 656.20 to proposed section 656.13, again further revising them to create clear employer attestations in efforts to clarify and/or update compliance requirements. Finally, the Department also proposes new attestations to reflect new requirements through this proposed rule. The proposals in this rule strengthen U.S. worker protections and bolster program integrity by holding employers who choose to participate in the PERM program accountable to the Department, and to their responsibilities to both U.S. workers and aliens, with regard to the employer’s filing of the Application for Permanent Employment Certification and participation in the PERM program.

Proposed new section 656.13(a) continues to require an employer seeking to permanently employ an alien to attest that the job opportunity is a bona fide, full-time, permanent position and adds that the terms and conditions of employment must comply with all applicable laws and regulations, consistent with current sections 656.10(c)(7) and (1). This proposed revision continues current sections 656.10(c)(5), (8), and (9) attestations, requiring the employer to attest that the job opportunity has been and is open to any qualified U.S. worker, any U.S. worker who applied was rejected for lawful, job- related reasons, and the job opportunity does not involve unlawful discrimination. The Department proposes to expand this attestation so that the job opportunities that are the subject of Applications for Permanent Employment Certification remain open to the employer’s laid off-employees in the place(s) of employment in the same or similar occupation throughout the period in which the employer is establishing its sponsorship of an alien for permanent employment in the United States—between filing the Application for Permanent Employment Certification and the date the Form I-140 petition is approved by USCIS or the date of determination, if the Application for Permanent Employment Certification or Form I-140 petition is denied or withdrawn, whichever is later, which would form the basis for the alien’s application for a visa and admission to the United States as a permanent resident.81 In addition, the provision adds language explicitly requiring employers to comply with Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits workplace discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin. Nothing in Title VII, “makes it illegal to discriminate on the basis of citizenship or alienage.” Espinoza v. Farah Mfg. Co., 414 U.S. 86, 95 (1973). The provision also adds language requiring compliance with the Antidiscrimination Provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act, 8 U.S.C. 81 INA section 212(a)(5)(A)(i)(I) (stating that the Secretary certifies that there are not “sufficient workers . . . at the time of application for a visa and admission to the United States”). Section 1324b, which prohibits discrimination because of citizenship status against protected individuals and, for employers not covered by Title VII, because of national origin. That law states that it is an unfair immigration-related employment practice to discriminate against a citizen or national of the United States based on their citizenship status. 8 U.S.C. § 1324b(a)(1), (3).
Separately, and under the Department’s own authority in 8 U.S.C.

1182(a)(5)(A)(i)(II), proposed section 656.13(a)(5) requires employers to offer U.S. workers terms, conditions, and privileges of employment no less favorable than those offered to the alien. Compliance with the PERM requirements is a floor; it does not establish compliance with Title VII or 8 U.S.C. 1324b, and a departure from the PERM requirements may be relevant evidence in an enforcement action or private suit under those laws. This provision will prohibit an employer from rejecting any qualified U.S. worker over a prospective alien based on any cost justifications or basis, including differences in any term, condition, or privilege of employment, and compensation and fringe benefits between any qualified U.S. worker and a prospective alien. This proposed provision is necessary to ensure the integrity of the PERM program by prohibiting situations where the job offer is designed to match the skills of a particular alien. Unduly restrictive job postings have a chilling effect on the number of qualified U.S. workers who respond to job vacancy postings, and the Department will prohibit this practice with this proposal. These proposals strengthen U.S. worker protections and bolster program integrity by holding U.S. employers who participate in the program accountable to the Department and U.S. workers beyond the processing of the Application for Permanent Employment Certification.

Under proposed section 656.13(b), the Department continues the attestation required under current section 656.10(c)(6) to require the employer to attest that the job opportunity is not vacant due to a strike or employees being locked out in the course of a labor dispute involving a work stoppage. The proposal, however, expands the strike provision of the current regulation to clarify that it covers “all places of employment” included on the Application for Permanent Employment Certification, including third- party employers’ locations. Through this proposed revised provision, the Department will improve program integrity and strengthen protections for U.S. workers.

To protect the integrity of the PERM labor certification program, deter fraud, and comply with the Department’s statutory obligation to protect the wages of U.S. workers, the Department is proposing in section 656.13(c) to revise and clarify the already- required attestations in current sections 656.10(c)(1) through (4). For example, current section 656.10(c)(1) requires the employer to attest that it has offered, and will continue to offer, a wage that equals or exceeds the PWD. Proposed section 656.13(c) would more clearly state the employer’s attestation that it has offered, and will continue to offer, a wage that equals or exceeds the highest of the Federal, State or local minimum wage or the PWD issued to the employer. The proposed paragraph clarifies that the offered wage requirement includes consideration of Federal, State, and local minimum wage rates, which is an existing requirement—for compliance with local, State, and Federal laws— under current section 656.10(c)(7). In addition, added content about the potential for an updated PWD reflects the potential for OFLC to obtain a new PWD, for example, during supervised recruitment. Further, this proposed provision adds new language stating that the offered wage cannot result in less favorable treatment of current or prospective U.S. workers in any terms, conditions, and privileges of employment, including compensation and fringe benefits, as compared with the alien (i.e., must not be lower than the wage the employer pays, and the wage the employer advertises, for similarly situated positions). A violation of this certification is a serious matter that will result in denial and may result in revocation, debarment, and referral under 656.31 and 656.32. The Department solicits comments on this proposed provision, including how this attestation could be worded more clearly to ensure that wage compensation and other benefits for U.S. workers similarly employed are not adversely affected by the prospective employment of the alien(s) in the job opportunity. The proposed attestation continues to specify that the offered wage cannot be based on commissions, bonuses or other incentives, unless the employer guarantees an offered wage earned on a weekly, bi-weekly, or monthly basis that equals or exceeds the prevailing wage. The Department proposes expanding the attestation to accommodate the possibility of the Department issuing a new or revised PWD (e.g., post-filing supervised recruitment) and, if so, the employer would be required to update its wage offer, unless notified otherwise by the Department.

The Department also proposes to continue to require the employer to attest that it has enough funds available to pay the offered wage for work performed in the job opportunity at the time of Application for Permanent Employment Certification submission. The Department proposes to revise this attestation for clarity and to include the citation to DHS’s requirements regarding the employer’s ability to pay at 8 CFR 204.5(g)(2), as USCIS will assess the employer’s compliance during I-140 Petition review. These revisions would better apprise employers of this requirement, while avoiding duplicative regulatory provisions. In addition, citing to DHS’s regulations would reduce the potential for confusion about the assessment to be performed when the employer files the I-140 Petition.

Under proposed section 656.13(d), the employer must attest that it has conducted, and will continue to conduct, recruitment of U.S. workers in good faith and in the same manner it normally recruits and considers U.S. workers in the same job opportunities that it does not request PERM labor certification, while also ensuring that its recruitment meets the standards set forth in proposed section 656.17. Through this proposed provision, the Department would require that the employer recruit U.S. workers in good faith and follow the same methods they would typically use for similar job opportunities where they do not seek PERM labor certifications for aliens, including when those methods they typically use for similar job opportunities exceed the requirements in proposed section 656.17. Where, how, and for how long an employer advertises a job opportunity in connection with the PERM labor certification program must be at least equal to the employer’s practices for similar job opportunities unrelated to a PERM labor certification. Similarly, the employer’s application process for candidates who apply for the employer’s job opportunity that is the subject of the PERM application, must not disadvantage U.S. workers or be less available to U.S. workers than the employer’s standard for same job opportunities that are unrelated to a request for PERM labor certification. Additionally, if required, interviews must be conducted by phone or arranged through other means (e.g., virtual meetings, cloud calls, or other platforms or applications that facilitate communication without involving physical presence) to minimize costs for U.S. workers and facilitate the process should the applicant, for example, be unable to travel or be physically present at the employer’s location for an interview. Further, the employer's representative who interviews or considers U.S. workers for the job offered to the alien must be a U.S. worker and one who normally interviews or considers, on behalf of the employer, applicants for job opportunities such as that offered the alien which do not involve labor certifications. Lastly, employers are prohibited from giving preferential treatment to aliens over U.S. workers concerning any requirements for applications and interviews related to the PERM application process. These attestations are necessary because there have been several reports of employers creating separate recruitment processes for PERM applications that deter U.S. workers from applying for job opportunities.82 In one instance, the Department of Justice 82 See, e.g., “Civil Rights Division Sues Cloudera for Excluding U.S. Workers from Applying to High- Paying Technology Jobs,” Dept. of Justice (Apr. 28, 2026), https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/civil-rights- division-sues-cloudera-excluding-us-workers-applying-high-paying-technology (alleging Cloudera intentionally created a separate recruitment and hiring process to deter U.S. workers from applying); Gooding, Dan, “Tech Companies Accused of Bending H-1B Rules with Newspaper Job Listings,” (DOJ) found that an employer did not advertise positions it sought to fill through the PERM program on its external job website, even though its standard practice was to post other job positions on this website.83 The employer also required all applicants for PERM-related positions to mail paper applications, even though the company permitted electronic applications for other positions.84 These provisions would clarify expectations for employer conduct during the PERM application recruitment process.

Currently, if the employer has a layoff in the AIE within six months of filing the Application for Permanent Employment Certification, the employer must document that it has notified and considered all of the employer’s potentially qualified laid off U.S. workers for the job opportunity to be offered in an Application for Permanent Employment Certification. See current section 656.17(k). The proposed rule would convert the existing layoff obligation into an employer attestation and relocate the provision to the newly proposed section 656.13(e) with revisions. As proposed, section 656.13(e)(1) would address layoffs prior to the employer’s filing of an Application for Permanent Employment Certification, while section 656.13(e)(2) would address post- filing layoffs.

The Department’s proposals regarding layoffs and consideration of laid-off U.S. workers are intended to provide U.S. workers additional protections against improper hiring conduct by employers85 and prevent employers from laying off U.S. worker(s) and creating vacancies which are then filled with aliens using the PERM process.86 As proposed, an employer would be required to attest that it has not laid off any U.S. worker(s) in the same or similar occupation that is the subject of the Application for Permanent Employment Certification in the area of intended employment of the place(s) of employment within 2 years prior to filing the application. The Department proposes to change the current term to describe similar occupations from “occupation for which certification is sought or in a related occupation” in current section 656.17(k) to “same or similar occupation” in proposed section 656.13(e), for readability. The Department does not intend for this proposed revision to change the employers’ consideration of their laid- off employees post-filing of the Application for Permanent Employment Certification and reminds employers that their obligation is to consider all potentially qualified laid-off U.S. workers for job opportunities that are the subject of a pending or certified Application for Permanent Employment Certification. The Department invites comments on this proposed change and ways to improve clarity.
